title: How Likely and How Deep? Sharp Joint Bounds on Risk-Neutral Crash Probability and Conditional Depth from Option Bid-Ask Quotes

p.t: How likely is a crash, and how deep will it be if it arrives? Index option prices bear directly on both questions, because an out-of-the-money put is directly exposed to losses below its strike. Under a risk-neutral measure Q, for a terminal index level 𝑋 normalized by its forward and a threshold 𝐾 < 1, define where 𝐿 𝐾 is the normalized put value and hence an unconditional shortfall, while 𝑠 𝐾 is the average shortfall below 𝐾 given that the threshold is breached. With finitely many strikes and nonzero bid-ask spreads, neither 𝑝 𝐾 nor 𝑠 𝐾 is point-identified, and the harder problem is joint. Since 𝐿 𝐾 = 𝑝 𝐾 𝑠 𝐾 , a frequent breach concentrated just below 𝐾 can carry the same put value as a rarer and deeper one. Sharp intervals computed separately for probability and depth intervals as primitive and selects the smoothest compatible density by quadratic programming. Wizman et al. (2026) combine arbitrage filtering with a smoothness and entropy criterion to select a density from short-dated bid-ask quotes. Starting from discrete arbitrage-free prices rather than original quote intervals, Qin et al. (2026) select admissible strike slopes and construct a marginal that reprices every input exactly. We instead retain every distribution compatible with the finite bid-ask box. The distinction is substantive: a selection criterion resolves observational equivalence, whereas our purpose is to measure it.

The mathematical foundation is the model-free bounds literature. Bertsimas and Popescu (2002) formulate sharp option-price bounds under moment information as generalized moment problems and derive converse moment bounds from option prices. King et al. (2005) develop calibrated option bounds. Finite-strike consistency and exact calibration are studied by Davis and Hobson (2007); Cousot (2007). In the one-asset case, Bertsimas and Bushueva (2006) reduce bounds for continuous piecewise-linear payoffs to linear optimization. Probability bounds based on finitely many options appear in Bassett (1997). Cohen et al. (2020) propose sparse linear-programming repair of option quotes within bid-ask bounds. Discontinuous contingent claims can exhibit nonattainment and sensitivity to boundary mass under finite strike information (Cox and Obłój, 2011). Liang et al. (2026) show that bounds for digital payoffs have a sharp square-root response as bid-ask spreads vanish. Our threshold coordinate preserves this type of boundary effect in the finite-dimensional joint probability-loss projection. The closest computational work includes Barratt et al. (2024). They optimize CDF and conditional probability bounds over discretized risk-neutral probabilities, derive VaR bounds from the CDF bounds, and formulate a problem for the CVaR upper bound. De Vries (2026) construct projection estimators based on option portfolios for general payoffs, apply them to indicator payoffs to obtain a pricing-consistent CDF, and derive a finite-sample approximation bound. That method targets an estimator under a chosen projection weight; our target is the full feasible set under the observed bid-ask intervals. van Eekelen (2023) derives sharp generalized-moment bounds for conditional expectations; our object instead identifies the conditioning probability jointly with its shortfall numerator. Neufeld et al. (2023) develop algorithms that compute 𝜀-optimal bounds for continuous piecewise-affine payoffs; non-CPWA payoffs such as digitals first require approximation. Polyhedral enumeration in objective space by repeated supporting linear programs, including primal and dual outer approximation, is longstanding in multiobjective optimization (Ehrgott et al., 2012). Support-function representations of compact convex identified sets and objective-space formulations of polyhedral projection are likewise established (Beresteanu and Molinari, 2008;Löhne and Weißing, 2016). Our adaptive two-dimensional hull routine builds on these methods; what is new is its target, a vanilla representation with explicit threshold mass whose projection gives the entire sharp joint ( 𝑝, 𝐿) polygon. The polygon then maps analytically into conditional depth.

A related empirical literature extracts disaster and tail information (Backus et al., 2011;Bollerslev and Todorov, 2011). Parametric tail estimates based on extreme value theory include Vilkov and Xiao (2013), and O'Sullivan and Wang (2018) jointly estimate risk-neutral tail probabilities and tail expectations beyond observed strike bounds. Bounds on physical crash probabilities require restrictions linking physical and risk-neutral measures; Martin and Shi (2026), for example, impose a stochastic discount factor based on power utility and then bound over dependence structures consistent with option-implied marginals. Our analysis remains entirely under Q. Finally, the fixed-threshold depth 𝑠 𝐾 is distinct from quantile-based tail measures. It coincides with CVaR when 𝐾 is the relevant quantile and boundary mass is treated by the tail-average convention (Rockafellar and Uryasev, 2000). Our object fixes 𝐾 and retains the full joint set implied by the original quote intervals. 3 Market setup and the joint tail object

p.s: A finite representation with explicit threshold mass
p.t: The finite representation has a simple division of labor. Cell mass and first moment price every retained vanilla payoff; one additional coordinate assigns threshold mass to the event; and the quote box selects admissible moment vectors. Theorem 4.2 shows that these three ingredients suffice to recover the joint object exactly.

Thus every bid-ask restriction is linear in (𝑧, 𝑚). Every retained vanilla payoff is affine on each cell, so its expectation depends only on the cell masses and first moments. Lemma A.1 in Appendix A.1 proves the converse: every vector satisfying (7)-( 9) is generated by unit-mean measures in the closure. Thus (10) is exact without an outcome grid. When the nonzero conditional cell means lie in the relative interiors of their cells, placing each cell mass at 𝑚 𝑗 /𝑧 𝑗 gives an attaining measure with finite support.

The dual of (15) attaches multipliers to bid, ask, mass, first-moment, cell, and threshold-atom constraints. Strong duality gives the same support value in both programs. For the sign convention in (15), the dual is Quote, cell, atom, and (when present) common budget constraints contribute distinct blocks of 𝜆. For each exposed boundary point, an optimal dual solution decomposes the support bound into cash and forward terms, a signed portfolio of retained quote endpoints, and nonnegative structural cell terms. Quote constraints with nonzero multipliers identify which intervals enter the certificate. p.s: Why an outcome grid can fail at the threshold
p.t: An outcome-grid method replaces Q by probabilities on fixed nodes. This is natural for continuous payoffs but delicate for 𝑝 𝐾 . Proposition 5.1 (Threshold non-uniformity). Fix a mass parameter 0 < 𝛼 < 1. For every sufficiently small 𝜀 > 0, there exist pairs of distributions whose call-price vectors at any finite collection of strikes differ by 𝑂 (𝜀), while their values of Q(𝑋 ≤ 𝐾) differ by 𝛼, obtained by placing mass 𝛼 at 𝐾 -𝜀 versus 𝐾 + 𝜀. The coordinatewise interval hull of the two call vectors has width 𝑂 (𝜀), while its compatible 𝑝 𝐾 values remain 𝛼 apart. Thus convergence of vanilla option prices alone does not imply convergence of sharp CDF bounds at an atomic threshold. The proposition pins down when discretizing the state space changes a discontinuous target. It is the reason the continuous-state formulation carries the threshold mass explicitly.

p.s: Data and empirical design 6.1 SPX panels
p.t: The application uses SPX call and put bid-ask quote files in OptionMetrics format from 2 January 2013 through 31 August 2023. Normalization uses the SPX level and a panel-level forward estimate for the selected date and maturity. The robustness analysis applies multiplicative shifts of ±20 basis points. The sampling rule selects one eligible panel per calendar week. Wednesday is preferred; if it is absent or ineligible, the order is Tuesday, Monday, Thursday, Friday. Both a short expiry (7-21 days, closest to 14) and a medium expiry (22-60 days, closest to 45) must be available, with at least 18 distinct put strikes in log-moneyness [-0.35, 0.05]. Ties are resolved in favor of the earlier expiry. The resulting sample has 557 dates from 2 January 2013 to 30 August 2023; 98.92% are Wednesdays. We retain positive strikes, nonnegative bids, positive asks, noncrossed bid-ask pairs, and expiries between 7 and 120 days. The primary information sets use puts converted by parity; a call-put panel is reserved for robustness. The complete eligible wing comprises all puts in the selected date-expiry panel satisfying these filters and having log-moneyness in [-0.35, 0.05]. Multiple retained observations at the same strike remain separate constraints.

The main thresholds are 𝐾 ∈ {0.85, 0.90}. They represent forward-normalized declines of 15% and 10%. We analyze: (i) the wedge-adjusted product of separate marginal bounds; (ii) the nearest puts at or below and at or above 𝐾 (vertical pair); if both select a quote exactly at 𝐾, retain that strike and the next-nearest distinct strike by absolute distance; (iii) the vertical pair plus the six nearest remaining put strikes (local eight); (iv) the complete eligible put wing. For the relaxation analysis, write the complete-wing reference set as I 𝐶 . If it has 𝑁 𝐶 distinct strikes and 𝑛 𝐶 (𝑘 𝑖 ) observations at strike 𝑘 𝑖 , we use Thus each distinct strike receives equal total weight, divided equally across observations at that strike. In the primary hard regime, when the baseline area is positive, the identification gain from set 𝐴 to the complete wing is Positive Δ 𝐴 is the fractional contraction in transformed area from the additional quotes and satisfies 0 ≤ Δ 𝐴 ≤ 1 in exact arithmetic. Larger values indicate stronger identification relative to the baseline set. Sensitivity calculations use the same formula with R 𝐴 𝐾 , δ in place of R 𝐴 𝐾 . Feasibility under the original bid-ask constraints is the primary criterion and holds in 93.90% of the 2,228 complete-wing cases. Assumption 4.1 holds in 2,076 of these cases. Panels with ambiguous contract identity are excluded, leaving 1,966 cases in the primary empirical sample. Sixteen feasible cases fail Assumption 4.1, and 136 cases are infeasible without relaxation and therefore enter the separately reported common-budget analysis.

We form percentile intervals for median identification gains from 2,000 draws of a circular moving-block bootstrap. If 𝑛 is the number of sampled dates in a primary horizon-threshold cell, the rule round(𝑛 1/3 ) gives eight chronologically ordered dates per block in each primary cell. Resampling dates rather than individual quotes preserves market panels and allows short-range serial dependence (Lahiri, 2003). Robustness checks target four design choices: the probability floor, forward and spread inputs, strike and duplicate selection, and the maturity-threshold grid. Probability-floor results reuse the reconstructed polygons; the additional checks use selected date subsamples. Appendix A.3 summarizes the specifications. ), with 𝑝 0 = 10 -4 . Larger entries indicate greater contraction relative to the stated baseline. For each threshold, there are 535 primary short-horizon cases and 448 primary medium-horizon cases, giving 1,966 cases in total. Intervals use 2,000 circular-block draws with eight chronologically ordered dates satisfying the primary-sample conditions per block. Each point estimate uses the midpoint of its numerical area interval. Intervals are pointwise descriptive summaries of sampling variation; numerical optimization error is assessed separately.

Table 1 summarizes identification gains in the primary sample. Across the four horizon-threshold cells, the complete wing contracts the area of the local eight by 5.35% to 18.16% at the median. Quotes beyond the local eight therefore eliminate between one-twentieth and one-fifth of the joint ambiguity that the nearby strikes leave open. The economic content of this contraction is global rather than local. Quotes away from 𝐾 restrict where the common risk-neutral distribution can place compensating probability and first moment while keeping every modeled price inside its interval and satisfying E Q [𝑋] = 1. A reallocation that fits nearby strikes can therefore fail elsewhere on the wing. The complete wing disciplines the feasible probability-depth combinations; it does more than refine local interpolation at 𝐾. Across complete-wing cases in the primary sample, the median ratio of joint area to the area of the wedge-adjusted marginal benchmark is 0.6340. In the median case, 36.6% of the transformed benchmark area is therefore unattainable: separate sharp marginals, even combined with the algebraic inequality 𝐿 ≤ 𝐾 𝑝, admit many probability-depth pairs that no single quote-compatible distribution can generate. Within the primary sample, complete-wing median probability widths are 0.00448 and 0.01055 at the short horizon, and 0.01904 and 0.03699 at the medium horizon, for 𝐾 = 0.85 and 0.90, respectively. Marginal probability uncertainty therefore remains visible even when joint restrictions sharply reduce the probability-depth region.

Figure 1 displays the representative case used for the dual certificate: the short-horizon panel dated 5 July 2017, with maturity 19 July 2017 and 𝐾 = 0.90. It satisfies the original quote constraints and Assumption 4.1.

Appendix Table A1 reports subperiod summaries and results that exclude the calibration dates, both under the primary sample definition. The median area ratio varies little across subperiods. Median identification gains remain positive under prespecified perturbations to forwards, quotes, strike coverage, horizons, and thresholds; Appendix Table A2 reports the range of median ratios for each specification. One caution applies when reading these ratios: the denominator is itself a moving marginal wedge, so doubled spreads can lower the ratio even as absolute probability widths increase. 8 Outcome-grid benchmark and dual evidence

The benchmark follows the outcome-grid approach of Barratt et al. (2024). We use 51, 101, 201, and 401 nodes; support caps of 2 and 3; and two treatments of 𝐾: inserting it as a node or centering it in a cell. Each specification contains 32 empirical panel-threshold cases and four synthetic atomic cases, for 36 cases in total. Let 𝑐 index a case and 𝑔 a grid specification. Let 𝛿 ★ grid,𝑔,𝑐 be the minimum weighted quote loss for its grid formulation, and let 𝛿 ★ cont,𝑐 be the continuous-state minimum computed before imposing the support cap. For each (𝑔, 𝑐), let Under each grid and support-cap specification, the discrete and continuous programs use the same quote loss budget and are evaluated in the same 64 directions. Support errors therefore compare the two state representations at the same grid-specific relaxation budget. Because 𝛿 𝑔,𝑐 varies with the grid, cross-grid changes combine grid refinement with changes in the relaxation budget. Table A3 reports the increment over 𝛿 ★ cont,𝑐 : it is material at 51 nodes (median (1.22-1.63) × 10 -4 for cap 2) and falls to the numerical 10 -10 floor at 201 and 401 nodes in the cap-2 median. Figure 2 separates typical from worst-case error. Median error declines strongly and is numerically zero with 𝐾 inserted and 401 nodes. The maximum, however, remains 0.15. Centering 𝐾 in a cell lowers this plateau to approximately 0.075. Both plateaus are generated by the synthetic 0.15 threshold atom; the inserted-node plateau equals that mass, whereas the centered-cell plateau is approximately half as large. Grid density therefore improves typical continuous-payoff approximation while the event convention continues to govern atomic cases. An inserted node assigns all of its mass to {𝑋 ≤ 𝐾 }; representing limiting mass immediately to its right requires a separate one-sided threshold state. In the subset of real SPX panels at support cap 2, the maximum error falls from 0.0751 to 0.0100 for centered grids and from 0.0784 to 0.0138 when 𝐾 is inserted. The persistent overall maxima therefore come from the atomic counterexample; errors on typical panels decline with refinement.

p.s: Primal-dual verification and a dual certificate
p.t: For the representative case, primal-dual gaps and KKT residuals are below 2 × 10 -14 in the directions that maximize frequency, loss, and the frequency-loss trade-off. At a 10 -8 multiplier threshold, the certificate for each direction uses two material quote endpoints; the remaining terms enforce mass, cell-moment, and threshold-atom restrictions. Figure 3 displays an optimal trade-off dual certificate.

Option-implied crash probability and conditional depth are identified jointly, not separately. Marginal intervals erase the trade-off that a common risk-neutral distribution imposes; the probability-depth frontier preserves it. Under Assumption 4.1, the frontier has a finite linear representation with explicit threshold mass, and support programs recover its boundary along with dual certificates at the quote level. In more than ten years of weekly SPX panels, the complete put wing contracts transformed area by 5.4-18.2% relative to the local eight and by 74.3-89.0% relative to the vertical pair. Strikes away from the threshold therefore carry material information about which joint tail scenarios remain compatible with the market. Outcome grids are not a substitute. Their median errors decline sharply with refinement, but worst-case errors at atomic thresholds persist because the event indicator is discontinuous; the continuous-state frontier handles that boundary directly. The frontier converts a finite option panel into valuation bounds, market-implied stress scenarios, comparisons across strike sets, and certificates that trace each reported boundary value back to observed quotes.
